sourceInformation.tech: Three.js 0.180.0 WebGPURenderer (WebGL2 fallback), Rapier 0.19.3, Gamepad API, Web Audio, WebRTC, AI Hub Session Protocol v1 client 1.4.0; one HTML file with CDN engine dependencies
sourceInformation.artDirection: Procedural cel-shaded 3D tabletop diorama with ink outlines, cream paper, teal and vermilion
sourceInformation.animation: Three.js AnimationMixer and AnimationClip for treads, antenna and cannon recoil; procedural particles and motion
sourceInformation.audio: Code-synthesized funk music (10% default), effects, and Animalese-style formant gibberish voices; no audio files
sourceInformation.online: AI Hub shared-world two-player host-authoritative sessions; standalone direct WebRTC invitation/return codes; local two-player duel
sourceInformation.testing: Headless Chromium 153 with native WebGPU; file and HTTP loading; scripted nine-wreck circuit through real Rapier physics; keyboard/mouse, emulated standard gamepads and multitouch; 17 offline-audio checks; two-browser WebRTC and four AI Hub harness scenarios; visual review. Physical devices and listening: unknown.
sourceInformation.research: none; native source knowledge only. Supplied AI Hub integration code and pinned engine distributions downloaded directly.

testingFeedback: Automated testing caught three game defects: pause-overlay routing, missed fast action taps, and menu accept/back presses blocked by the navigation-repeat timer. It also isolated one software-WebGPU launch-configuration issue. Static review found additional UI and network edge cases, which were corrected.
One game defect blocked a required flow: the pause and developer menus. The graphics failure belonged to the test configuration, and was reproduced in a minimal Three.js scene.
The scripted nine-wreck circuit used real Rapier impacts through all three arenas. The four AI Hub harness scenarios were the most useful network lifecycle checks.
Early screenshots under the failing software-WebGPU flags showed a blank canvas; a minimal engine scene was more useful for isolating the configuration problem.
engineFeedback: Three.js made procedural dioramas, toon shading, orthographic cameras and native AnimationMixer clips work together cleanly. Rapier supplied reliable collision and ricochet behavior.

The initially supplied software-WebGPU adapter flag destroyed the device even in a minimal Three.js scene. Alternate Vulkan/ANGLE flags resolved it. Fast input taps also needed explicit queuing between physics ticks.
The fixed-step tank simulation, AI navigation and bank-shot selection, controller-first menus, arena rules and authoritative network state.
Coordinating browser input, fixed-step physics, native animation, and host/client lifecycle across WebGPU, touch and controller paths.
none; the engine libraries are unmodified. Materials, clips, physics rules and renderer settings are application code.
A built-in controller-first menu and focus system, with clear WebGPU device diagnostics, would simplify this kind of small game.
promptFeedback: The source, visual style, controller-first direction and complete vertical-slice requirements gave a clear creative target. The testing stand-ins made headless verification practical.

The prohibition on internet research coexists with a required remote integration. I treated direct downloads of the supplied integration code and pinned engine distributions as implementation, and did no source research.
Making the complete solo, couch, touch and online flows behave consistently, including attract mode and network end states.
Specify whether manual WebRTC code exchange is acceptable for standalone play and whether a relay or matchmaking service is available.

aiHub.name: ComBop
aiHub.description: A playful ink-and-paper tank rumble inspired by Combat. Bank shells around corners, vanish in the ghost garden, and burst through a three-arena solo circuit or duel a friend.
aiHub.controls: WASD / left stick move; mouse / right stick aim; click / R2 fire; Space / Circle / L2 burst; Esc / Options pause; touch drag to drive with assisted fire.
